items.summary:
Christopher Woolcott has today been given a 2-year prison sentence, suspended for 2 years, after staging a £154m fake takeover bid for Touchstone Exploration Inc.

items.title: UK financial watchdogs clarify cyber expectations as attacks rise
items.summary:
UK’s financial regulators are proposing new guidance to help financial services firms prepare for and recover from cyber incidents as threats grow.

The Bank of England’s most recent Systemic Risk Survey cited cyber as one of the risks that would have the greatest impact on the UK financial system. October 2026 saw the second-highest monthly number of cyber incidents reported to the FCA in 5 years, and the highest in the past 18 months, 52% above the previous high recorded in May 2025.In response, the Bank, FCA and Prudential Regulation Authority (PRA) are bringing together existing requirements and lessons from supervisory experience to give firms greater clarity about what is expected of them.The proposed guidance aligns with recognised cyber frameworks, including the National Cyber Security Centre’s (NCSC) Cyber Assessment Framework. It sets out how firms should manage their cyber risk and resilience without imposing rigid rules, giving firms flexibility in how they meet the expectations in a fast-evolving threat environment.It covers key areas, including how firms govern, identify, protect against, detect, respond to and recover from cyber risks and incidents. items.title: FCA launches world-first platform giving firms new insight into AI innovation
items.summary:
New resource brings together real-world examples of AI adoption across financial services, helping firms identify emerging trends and opportunities.

The FCA has launched a world-first AI Spotlight Observatory that provides firms, academics and innovators with a comprehensive view of how AI is being adopted across financial services.Based on practical use cases from more than 200 organisations and spanning 150 areas of activity, the online platform highlights how firms are using AI across the industry and where trends are developing.Developed in partnership with the Centre for Finance, Technology and Entrepreneurship (CFTE) and technology partner NayaOne, the Observatory helps meet the growing demand for greater visibility of AI adoption across the sector.The resource highlights a range of AI use cases shaping financial services, from solutions designed to combat financial crime and enhance compliance processes to emerging technologies such as agentic payments and neurosymbolic AI.By widening access to market intelligence, the Observatory will help firms of all sizes learn from developments across the market, better understand emerging technologies and make more informed decisions

items.title: Insurance firms called on to improve claims handling
items.summary:
The FCA and Financial Ombudsman Service have published a report setting out what insurers need to focus on to ensure claims are dealt with promptly, clearly and fairly.

We are helping firms learn from Financial Ombudsman complaints and strengthen their claims handling in line with our existing rules to improve service quality for insurance customers.The report highlights where claims handling can improve and explains the key rules firms need to meet.Building on findings in our 2025 review of home and travel insurance, it calls on insurers to:Keep claims moving.Give customers clear and timely updates.Take responsibility when problems arise with third parties working on their behalf.While 79% of people who make a claim are satisfied with claims handling (PDF), improvements are needed in consumer understanding and service quality.Chris Knight, director for insurance at the FCA, said: 'Most insurance customers receive a good service, but we know there is room for improvement – and when standards fall short, firms must put things right. items.title: Bereaved families need support, not a battle with paperwork
items.summary:
Investment firms must do more to help people dealing with the death of a loved one, after a review found confusing communications, delays and gaps in support.

The FCA reviewed how financial advisers, wealth managers and investment platforms support bereaved families and those handling someone’s estate.Some firms provided thoughtful, personal support. Others had processes that risked adding to people’s distress and financial pressure.Some firms left people unclear about what to do next or offered limited ways to get in touch. In some cases, advice fees were still being taken until an original death certificate was provided.Kate Tuckley, head of department, consumer investments at the FCA, said, 'Dealing with someone’s finances after a death should not mean a battle with paperwork. items.summary:
